title: Develop at Idea Velocity - Jeffrey Lee-Chan, Snapchat
talk_summary: A workshop-style demo of one engineer's personal agent setup (OpenClaw + tmux + worktrees + Codex) for high-velocity solo development, with Q&A. Most content is tooling tour and live debugging; the transferable ideas are context separation between manager and worker agents, worktree-based parallelism, and tiered model fallback.

takeaways.technique: Manager/worker context separation to remove self-review bias
takeaways.what_they_do: Runs a separate 'manager' agent in its own terminal whose context is specs/priorities/PR history rather than the implementation, so it judges worker output skeptically instead of rubber-stamping it.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the manager has a different context um than the workers

takeaways.technique: Git worktrees per agent for parallel work
takeaways.what_they_do: Each parallel agent gets its own worktree so multiple agents can build simultaneously without stepping on each other's checkout.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I use multiple agents with work trees, that's very key for parallelization

takeaways.technique: Tiered model fallback by quota, not preference
takeaways.what_they_do: Uses a strong model (Codex 5.3) as default, and when quota runs low switches to a cheaper/weaker model (MiniMax) that 'gets the job done', accepting quality drop for cost.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I use this until like this is getting low and then I just switch to MiniMax, which is not as good, but it kind of gets the job done

takeaways.technique: Keep implementation context out of the planning agent
takeaways.what_they_do: Deliberately keeps the orchestrating agent's context about specs, goals, and recent task history rather than code/skills/MCP boilerplate, arguing ~25% of a coding agent's context is consumed by implementation scaffolding.
takeaways.evidence_quote: imagine like 25% of your context already taken up by implementation
takeaways.numbers: ~25% of context consumed by implementation scaffolding (speaker's estimate)

takeaways.technique: Layered test ladder ending in browser/visual tests
takeaways.what_they_do: Pushes verification down a ladder — unit/API-level tests without a browser, then MCP/HTTP checks, then browser tests only for genuinely visual behavior — and re-evaluates quarterly which steps still need a human.
takeaways.evidence_quote: which problems truly needed that human or not

takeaways.technique: Staging instance for integration tests, not duplicate work
takeaways.what_they_do: Runs a second isolated instance as staging; explicitly warns not to send the same task to both (doubles tokens) but to develop locally and run integration tests against staging before merging to prod.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I would do local development and then I would run integration tests on the um sandbox or staging one
